idiom_name: recursive split/solve/combine with pthread fork/join (or OpenMP tasks where the toolchain provides them)
implementation_notes: ISO C has no task substrate, so the whole structure is explicit: a recursive function that tests the base case, splits the range, and either recurses sequentially below the cut-off or forks a worker thread for one half and joins it before combining. pthread_create/pthread_join give only the fork and the join - there is no work stealing, no task queue and no automatic load balancing - so a hand-rolled version either forks only at shallow depth or sits on an explicit work queue. Where the toolchain ships an OpenMP runtime, #pragma omp task with #pragma omp taskwait replaces the pthread plumbing; the recursive structure stays exactly the same, the runtime owns the pool.
pitfalls: pthreads do not work-steal: a fork/join that creates one thread per subproblem oversubscribes the CPU and is usually slower than the sequential recursion.
The join orders threads but does not protect memory: partial results written into a shared buffer still need their own mutex or atomic discipline.
Recursion depth is only logarithmic while the split is balanced; an unbalanced split - or attacker-controlled input - overflows the default stack.
